summary: For children aged 8–9 classifying materials as solids, liquids or gases. The core objective is to sort by BEHAVIOUR rather than appearance, using three reliable tests: does it keep its own shape (solid), does it take the shape of its container and form a level surface (liquid), does it spread out to fill all available space (gas)? Learners apply these tests to eight or more everyday materials and work the tricky cases that break naive rules: sand and powders (they pour but each grain is a solid that keeps its shape), steam (a gas, but the visible white cloud is condensed water droplets, not the invisible vapour), plus gels, foams and honey. Gases are made observable and tangible so 'gas is real stuff' is evidenced, not asserted. Explanations stay observational; the particle model is a light bridge, not a requirement at this stage.
misconceptions: Sorting by appearance — anything that pours (sand, salt, powder) is called a liquid, missing that each grain is a solid.
Gases are not matter / are weightless / are 'nothing', because they are usually invisible ('seeing is believing').
Believing the visible white cloud of 'steam' IS the water vapour, rather than tiny condensed droplets (the true vapour is invisible).
Thinking a liquid changes amount when it changes container shape (confusing shape with quantity).
Assuming very thick liquids (honey, gel) or very light solids (foam) can't be classified, or classifying them by feel rather than behaviour.

activities.title: Test the state bench: pour, seal, observe, sort
steps: Take each mystery substance and pour or place it into jars of different shapes; observe and record what happens.

Note which items keep the same shape in every jar (e.g. a wooden block) and which pool flat and take each jar's shape (e.g. water); then observe a gas swelling to fill a whole sealed jar (shown via a simulation/animation or a pre-prepared safe sealed demonstration — not a real coloured gas released in class), and see in the simulation that an open container would let the gas escape.
For the water, pour the same amount into several differently-shaped containers; confirm the shape changes while the amount stays the same.
Drop each tested item into a solid / liquid / gas bin and attach a short behaviour tag stating WHY (e.g. 'keeps its own shape', 'takes the jar's shape and lies flat', 'fills the whole space').

Test sand deliberately: pour it (it pours a bit like a liquid, but it heaps into a sloping pile instead of lying flat like water), then look closely at a single grain — note that each grain is hard and keeps its own shape, so classify sand as a solid because the GRAINS keep shape even though the pile pours.
activities.insight: A material's state is decided by how the material itself behaves (does it keep its own shape, take a container's shape, or fill all the space), not by whether it pours or how it looks. Sand pours but is a solid because each grain keeps its shape.

activities.title: Steam vs the white cloud
steps: With an adult handling the kettle safely, watch a boiling kettle and look for the small CLEAR gap right at the spout before the white cloud begins.
Before any reveal, predict which part is the actual gas (the real steam) and explain why.
Watch an adult hold a cold plate or spoon in the plume: observe droplets of liquid water forming on it.
State in your own words: the invisible part near the spout is the gas (water vapour); the white cloud higher up is tiny liquid droplets that have cooled and condensed.
activities.insight: True water vapour (steam) is an invisible gas; the visible white cloud above a kettle is tiny condensed liquid droplets, not the gas itself. 'I can see it, so that's the gas' is the belief to correct.

activities.title: Gas is real stuff
steps: Trap air by sealing a bag or squeezing a capped bottle; feel the resistance and note the gas takes up space.
Blow bubbles or feel a puff of air on your hand to sense that the invisible gas is really there.

Compare a ball pumped up hard (e.g. a football inflated with a pump) with the same ball when soft. If a sensitive balance is available, weigh it both ways: the hard-pumped ball should weigh slightly more because extra air has been squeezed in. Discuss whether the gas has mass. (A balloon blown up by mouth is not a good test: the air inside is barely squeezed, so a classroom balance will show little or no difference.)
Answer: can you see the air in this room? Is it still a gas even though it's invisible?
activities.insight: Gases are real matter: they take up space and have mass, even though they are usually invisible. An 'empty' sealed bottle is actually full of air.

activities.title: Classify and check: the eight-plus material sort
steps: Sort at least eight everyday materials into solid, liquid or gas, writing the behaviour reason for each.

Include genuinely tricky items — honey, jelly/gel, toothpaste, a solid foam such as a sponge — and decide each by behaviour rather than by how thick or light it feels; if an item shows both solid-like and liquid-like behaviour (e.g. toothpaste or shaving foam), record that it is a tricky mixture and describe what it does.
For each item answer 'which behaviour proves it?' by matching it to one of the three tests.
Explain aloud why sand is a solid and why the kettle cloud is not the gas.
activities.insight: Consistent behaviour-based criteria help classify awkward materials: very thick liquids (honey) and very light solids (solid foams such as a sponge or polystyrene) are judged by whether they keep their own shape, take a container's shape, or fill the space. Some materials, such as shaving foam, toothpaste or jelly, are mixtures that show some solid-like and some liquid-like behaviour, so it is fine to say they do not fit neatly.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Sand pours out of a bucket just like water does. Is sand a solid, a liquid, or something in between — and why?' Then: 'Now think about the white cloud you see above a boiling kettle. Is that cloud the gas (the steam itself), or is it something else?'
checkAnswer: Sand is a SOLID: it's made of many tiny solid grains, each keeping its shape; the pile pours only because the grains slide over one another. The white cloud above a kettle is NOT the gas — true steam (water vapour) is invisible; the white cloud is tiny liquid droplets that have condensed as the vapour cooled.
